newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr near breakdown from rate fatigue.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr near breakdown from rate fatigue.

text.p: The Australian dollar skidded to fresh 16-month lows Tuesday, snapping key chart support and threatening a whole new phase in its three month-old slide.

Traders said the US$0.7500/05 bulwark had been weakened by rate fatigue as the market drove down yields in anticipation of an official easing. It finally gave way offshore as a mob of Swiss, German and New York banks sold in serious size.

Tokyo names added to the pressure today by dumping AUD/yen and it was left to corporate bids to hold a ragged line at US$0.7480. Analysts doubted this would last long and looked for a test of US$0.7450 enroute to an eventual return to 73 cents.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the local dollar was face down at US$0.7480/85 having slipped from US$0.7513/18 late here Monday and 76 cents this time last week.
The dip took it below 75 cents for the first time since February 1996 and brought losses since the surprise Reserve Bank rate cut on May 23 to around three cents or almost four percent.

The start of the entire downtrend can be traced back to a peak of US$0.8005 in mid-March, so total losses amount to more than five cents or 6.5 percent. In trade weighted terms the decline has been even steeper at around 7.8 percent, which could have implications for imported inflation if sustained.

And the latest break meant there was more to come, with some analysts seeing scope for a decline to the 1996 trough of 73 cents. There were support levels ahead including US$0.7450, US$0.7420, US$0.7380 and US$0.7350, but analysts felt the low point would act as a major attractor now.

Today's domestic housing data provided a glimmer of light amongst the recent econoic gloom with dwelling commencements rising 4.6 percent in the March quarter to their highest levels in two years. Furthermore, starts in the December quarter were revised up to an increase of 8.3 percent from an intitially reported 5.9 percent gain.

The trend in starts also turned higher after dropping steadily from a peak in the June quarter of 1994. Analysts saw further gains ahead with housing finance running strong into Q2. But housing was one of all-too few sectors showing signs of responding to the RBA rate cuts already delivered and did little to shake market conviction the bank would ease again.

The lack of a move this morning did convince many the Bank would not act before its next board meeting on July 1 and 90-day bill futures pulled back six basis points in response to 94.83. That still implied a rate of 5.18 percent against the present 5.50 percent cash rate, illustrating the market's easing bias.
The next data of real importance are May retail trade and building approvals but these are not due until July 2.
On the crosses the currency lost ground to a strengthening yen to stand at 84.64/74 from 85.75/85 late Monday.
Dealers said the market had turned cautious in case Japanese trade data early Wednesday showed its surplus climbing to levels which would stoke trade tensions between it and the U.S.
The current account surplus is expected to balloon to around 549 billion yen in May from 229 billion a year earlier.
In trade weighted terms the dollar lurched to 56.7, its lowest close since August last year, from 57.1.
Elsewhere on the crosses, the local currency had slid to dangerous levels against its New Zealand counterpart in part due to a switch by offshore funds from the former to the latter.

The A$ hit a two-year low around NZ$1.0810 in early trade before bouncing to NZ$1.0847/62, but that was off from Monday's late NZ$1.0902/17 and far below the NZ$1.1300 level held before the RBA rate cut of May 23.

Analysts said the break of the NZ$1.0900/0924 support band was very bearish technically and unless it bounced soon the A$ was heading for NZ$1.0500 and even parity, an event New Zealand has long yearned to celebrate. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
